steps.title: Соедините слова и значения.
Два способа сказать «сейчас уже не так»
steps.html:
She used to leave the house at ten past seven. — привычка, которой больше нет.

She would walk the same route every morning. — та же привычка, но внутри рассказа.

The pattern used to run… — прошлое состояние, не привычка. Здесь возможно только used to.

steps.title: В каком предложении нельзя использовать would?
options: She left the house at seven every morning.
We had a factory in this street.
He walked the same route to work.
steps.answer: We had a factory in this street.
steps.why: Have здесь — состояние, а не повторяющееся действие. Можно used to have, но не would have.

steps.title: used to, would, Past Simple
steps.html:
ФормаКогда используемПример
used to + verbповторявшаяся привычка, теперь законченнаяShe used to leave at ten past seven.
used to + verbпрошлое состояние, которого больше нетThere used to be a factory here.
would + verbповторявшаяся привычка — но не состояниеShe would walk the same route every morning.
past simpleединичное событие или всё то же с указанием времениShe retired in 2004.
didn't use to / Did you use to…?отрицание и вопрос — обратите внимание на написаниеShe didn't use to question them.

steps.title: Как это работает
steps.html:
Обе формы говорят одно: это повторялось и больше не повторяется. Там, где речь о привычке, они взаимозаменяемы.

Разница — в состоянии. Used to подходит для состояний — I used to have a car. Would — нет.

Would к тому же требует, чтобы прошлое уже было задано. Рассказ не начинают с I would walk to school — начинают с used to, а дальше идёт would.

Есть второе used to, и это другое: be used to + -ing — «привык». I'm used to working late — про настоящее, не про прошлое.

steps.title: The way we used to work
steps.html:
Fifty years ago, most people expected one employer, one office and one pension. Almost every part of that has gone.

A  There was a time when a young person would leave school, walk into a local firm and stay there. My grandfather worked for the same company for forty-one years. He used to say that changing jobs looked unreliable — that an employer would want to know why you had left. The average worker today changes employer roughly every four to five years, and nobody asks that question any more.

B  Some occupations have disappeared entirely. Before alarm clocks were cheap, British factory towns employed knocker-uppers, who would walk the streets before dawn tapping on bedroom windows with a long stick until the sleeper appeared. Large offices had typing pools, where thirty or forty women would sit in rows typing what other people had written. Telegram boys, lift operators, lamplighters: none of these jobs was unskilled, and none of them exists now.

C  The working day was different too, and not always in the direction people imagine. Hours were long, but the boundaries were solid. When my grandfather left the building, he had left. There was no way for the office to reach him, and nobody expected it to. He used to describe his working conditions as hard but simple: you obeyed the rules, you followed the procedures, and in return the firm was supposed to look after you until you retired.

D  What replaced it is more relaxed and much less certain. Dress codes have almost gone. Many people can work from home, choose their own hours, or take a temporary contract that suits a particular year of their life. But the promise on the other side of that arrangement has gone as well. Very few employers now offer anything that resembles a lifetime, and the person who used to be looked after is expected to manage their own training, their own pension and their own reputation.

E  Whether this is progress depends on where you stand. People with skills that are in demand have never had more freedom: they can quit, negotiate, retrain or move country. People without them have inherited the insecurity without the freedom. The same change produced both outcomes, which is why arguments about modern work so often talk past each other.

F  My grandfather, who lived long enough to see the beginning of all this, was not nostalgic about it. He would point out that his forty-one years were not really a choice; there was nothing else, and leaving was frightening. “You had one life and one job,” he said, “and you hoped they suited each other.” What he valued was not the job. It was knowing, at twenty-five, roughly what the next forty years would look like — and that, more than any occupation, is what has actually disappeared.

People without them have inherited the insecurity without the freedom. The same change produced both outcomes, which is why arguments about modern work so often talk past each other.

F  My grandfather, who lived long enough to see the beginning of all this, was not nostalgic about it. He would point out that his forty-one years were not really a choice; there was nothing else, and leaving was frightening. “You had one life and one job,” he said, “and you hoped they suited each other.” What he valued was not the job. It was knowing, at twenty-five, roughly what the next forty years would look like — and that, more than any occupation, is what has actually disappeared.
